item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Still a bit ehhh on the scientific bits of this one.

"In male hosts, ova can develop into a larval stage. In female hosts, larval stage specimens may transition to the adult stage. Larvae introduced to male hosts and ova introduced to female hosts live at most three hours before expiring due to a lack of the hormones necessary for their further development."

This is extremely vague. Which hormones? The mention of men vs. women seems to suggest some typical "male" and "female" hormones, such as testosterone and estradiol. However, while the balance of these hormones is different, neither hormone is "lacking" in men or women, so it's extremely unrealistic that the parasite would perish because it wasn't getting enough of its hormone of choice. Develop more slowly, maybe, but not perish. Alternately, it would be much more creepier and more realistic (as this is something some actual parasites can do) if the parasite was able to influence the host's metabolic pathways to produce more of whatever hormone it needs.

item.title: "0.003% of infested males"
item.content:encoded:
The article on the whole was pretty good - but the line "Critical infestations have been seen to occur in 0.003% of infested males", implies that this SCP has infected a positively huge number of people.

The problem is that in order for that percentage to be known, it implies there are at least 1/0.00003, or ~30,000 known cases in males, of which, the critical infestation occurred only once. On top of that, it's known caseS, plural, meaning that multiple instances occurred.

For each critical instance, there are 60,000 non-critical instances, and due to the fact that it's written as a percentage, not "in three cases", this implies that there are a fairly large (tens to hundreds) number of critical infestations… for which, again, there are 60k normal infestations. This is a hugely, hugely widespread contagion in that case, and perhaps bigger than the intended feel of the SCP, given the intricate quarantine procedure required for treatment.

I'd suggest a minor edit to either:

  1. Bring it as a percentage closer to 0.03% or even 0.3%, meaning 1 in 6,000 people or even 1 in 600
  2. Instead of a percentage, use "in X recorded cases, what has been named a 'critical infestation' has occurred, where…" or something along those lines.
